opening.headline: The reason why only functions allowed by the administrator can be used is explained using control points called functions, connectors, and shares, and a role-based approach.
body: A plug-in that opens well on a colleague's screen is displayed as Disabled by admin on my screen, and some connectors are connected but others are blocked. If you don't know why, you won't know what to ask your manager.

In this lesson, we'll see that administrator control is divided into features, connectors and apps, and shares. Next, we'll compare the controls in the ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude admin consoles and see how permissions come together in role-based access. At the end, we explain the process for approving a new connector request and how to determine the reason when a request is blocked.

opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain administrator function control items
Separate control points for features, connectors, and sharing

screens.title: I can only use functions allowed by the administrator, but I don't know why.
screens.lead:
First, read about a situation where two people on the same team end up looking at different screens.

As of 2026-10: Gems are transitioning to skills. Personal accounts will be converted after November 2026, and Workspace business accounts will be converted after March 2027. The Gems screen below is based on the pre-migration environment. After moving the instructions and files, please check again for sharing and tool operation.

visual.alt: A comparison illustration of the screens of two people on the same team looking different.

paragraphs: Two employees from the same department use the same company workspace. My co-worker uses a certain plugin without a problem, but the same plugin is displayed as Disabled by admin on my screen. Connectors that can be connected also vary from person to person and app to app.

In cases like this, just telling the manager ‘no’ will result in a slow resolution. This is because the request varies depending on whether the cause of the blockage is because the function itself is turned off, because it is not included in my role, because the app attached to the plug-in is blocked, or because of sharing settings.
If you know what granularity administrator control is divided into, you can guess why. This class is a time to draw that map.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Is it a service error or a designed behavior that the screen is different for each person even though they are using the same service? You will answer this question again at the end of the lesson.

screens.outro: First, let me recall an experience where the AI function was blocked.

screens.title: Have you ever had an AI function blocked at your company?
screens.lead: If you first think about each question in your head and then select it, the instructor will organize your thoughts. You will not enter or submit an answer.

items.prompt: Have you ever found a feature you wanted to use not visible or inactive?
items.answer: New plug-ins and apps are usually disabled by default in Enterprise workspaces and are only opened after they are reviewed by an administrator. Not seeing a feature may not be an error, but rather an intended startup state.

items.prompt: Did you know then who was deciding it?
items.answer: The person who decides is the administrator of the workspace or organization. However, one person does not decide everything, and sometimes managers who turn on and off features, owners who create roles, and managers who set overall organization policies are responsible for each layer.

items.prompt: You just knew it was blocked, but did you check why?
items.answer: Knowing the reason makes your request specific. ‘Please turn on this feature’ and ‘Please open app access for this plugin in my role’ differ in the speed at which administrators process them. The goal of this class is to equip you with a way to narrow down the reasons.

screens.outro: Now let's take a look at what granularity administrator control is divided into.

screens.title: Control is divided into functional units
screens.lead: Select the arrows to cycle through the three units of administrator control and how different controls can apply to the same service.

visual.alt: An illustration of the three units of control listed from top to bottom: features, connectors and apps, and sharing, with a question attached to each.
labels: Which features should I turn on and off?
Which apps should be connected and what actions will be allowed?
How widely should projects and agents be shared?

steps.title: Functional approach
steps.body: Functional unit control determines who can use which functions. In ChatGPT, items such as model, GPT creation and sharing, canvas, project, memory, and link sharing are managed on a workspace-wide basis in Permissions & roles in Workspace settings.

steps.title: Connectors and Apps
steps.body: Connectors and per-app controls determine which external apps connect and what actions are allowed. ChatGPT reviews installation, app access, behavior, provider permissions, and content restrictions in Plugins in the Admin Console. New plugins and apps are largely disabled by default in Enterprise and Edu.

steps.title: share
steps.body: Sharing unit control determines how widely a project or agent is shared. For example, Claude administrators can turn off Share projects to prevent sharing projects with new users or groups, or just turn off Public projects.

steps.title: Multiple controls over the same service
steps.body: Control over the same service is not determined at once. In ChatGPT, installing plugins and accessing included apps are separate controls. So even if the plugin is installed, you may not be able to use the included app.

steps.title: Relationship between plugins and apps
steps.body: A plugin is a bundle of skills, apps, and app templates. Deactivating an app will prevent features that depend on the app, but it won't remove plugins or eliminate skills that don't depend on the app. Plugins that contain a required app inherit the roles and behavior settings of that app.

screens.outro: Let's now compare where the three products' administrator consoles handle this control.

screens.title: Control item correspondence table for 3rd company administrator consoles
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare where and what admins control in ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude.

tabs.label: ChatGPT
tabs.body: Workspace settings is the central screen for managing membership, seating defaults, feature access, GPT governance, apps, analytics, and identity controls. Plugins and marketplaces are managed in Plugins after selecting a workspace in the Admin Console. In Enterprise and Edu, new plugins and apps are usually disabled by default and opened by the administrator. In Business, the app is turned on by default and admins can change its availability across the workspace.

tabs.label: Gemini
tabs.body: In the Generative AI, Gemini for Workspace, Feature access panel of the Google Admin console, turn Gemini features on and off for each service, such as Gmail, Calendar, Drive and Docs, Meet, and Chat. The default is on. You can select an organizational unit or configuration group used as a departmental unit and apply it to only some users, and the group settings override the organizational unit settings. Gemini app access can be turned on and off separately.

tabs.label: Claude
tabs.body: Manage multiple locations in Organization settings. Connectors adds connectors to an organization, Data and privacy's Sharing section controls Share projects and Public projects, and Organization and access sets user provisioning and verified domain connector limits. In Enterprise, you can turn features such as Share projects on and off for each role in Roles.

tabs.label: Verified domain restrictions
tabs.body: Claude's Restrict verified-domain connectors to your enterprise setting prevents Claude accounts outside your organization from connecting specified connectors with your organization's verified domain emails. This setup connects your corporate Gmail to your personal Claude account to prevent corporate data from leaving your organization's control. This setting can be turned on in the Enterprise plan by Owners, Primary Owners, and custom roles with appropriate permissions.

tabs.label: common ground
tabs.body: All three products divide control into one or more units: features, connectors and apps, or shares, and narrow the scope by roles or organizational units. Since the name and location vary from product to product, it is quicker to first ask 'what unit does this control cover' rather than looking for the term on the screen.

screens.outro: Next, we will see how the scope of application is determined by role and organizational unit.

screens.title: Role-based access and coverage
screens.lead: When you select or hover over an underlined term, an explanation appears. See how roles and organizational units affect permissions.

data.text: In ChatGPT's role-based access control, Default, On, Off is used to represent the permission state of custom roles. A user can have multiple roles, and access is maintained as long as at least one role, such as Because authority is combined, is granted. Roles like Member, Admin, Owner (default role) define what can be managed rather than functional permissions. In Gemini, settings can be configured at the organizational unit or configuration group level, and even if Gemini is disabled in a service, How to access data from that service from other apps may still remain.

terms.tip: Default follows the workspace settings, On gives permission to that role, and Off does not give permission to that role. Access is maintained if other roles allow it.

The permissions of regular user-defined roles are additive. Whether it is a role given directly or through a group, you can access it if you allow one. Denied by regular RBAC only when all corresponding roles are Off.
Member, Admin, and Owner determine what members can manage. Access to features is determined by user-defined roles.
This is an advanced method to choose when applying settings to only some users in the Google Admin console. Group settings take precedence over organizational unit settings.

terms.term: How to access data from that service from other apps
terms.tip: For example, even if you turn off Gemini in Drive, people inside Gmail can still ask Gemini about Drive files. Turning off one service does not lose all access to your data.

screens.outro: We will now explain with an example the process by which a new connector request is approved.

screens.title: Commentary: How a new connector request is approved
screens.lead: The instructor explains the process from the perspective of the employee requesting a new connector and the manager reviewing it. Select the arrows and follow them step by step.

steps.title: 1. The requester writes down the task and required scope
steps.body: Instead of asking 'Please open the connector,' the requester asks the administrator by writing down what permissions are needed for what task. For example, write something like ‘I need to read the schedule and read the files in the designated folder to organize the meeting minutes.’

steps.title: 2. Administrator judges reading and writing
steps.body: Administrators determine whether reading alone is sufficient or whether writing tools such as sending mail or modifying files are also needed. For example, the Microsoft 365 connector has read search by default, and write tools must be turned on separately by your organization.

steps.title: 3. Open App Access and turn it on only for the roles you need.
steps.body: The administrator allows access to the app, but does not open it to everyone. In ChatGPT Enterprise and Edu, role-based access allows plug-in and app access to be divided by role, and the two controls are evaluated separately.

steps.title: 4. Check organizational policy conditions
steps.body: Confirm any conditions set by the organization. In Claude, you can't link a work email account to a personal account when verified domain restrictions are turned on, and how users are provisioned also determines how members enter your organization.

steps.title: 5. When the user connects, use the setting to request confirmation at first.
steps.body: Users connect to their account. At first, we used a setting that asks before reading and before changing, but once it is confirmed that the operation is reliable, we expand to a setting that does not ask for reading. Admin approval and user settings go hand in hand to create safety.

screens.outro: Now that you've seen the approval process, let's outline how to figure out why you're stuck.

screens.title: Explanation: The order of reasoning when you get stuck
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's commentary unfolds. This is a sequential order from top to bottom.

items.prompt: 1. Is the function itself turned off?
items.answer: The first thing to look at is whether the feature is turned off on a per-workspace basis. This is the most common reason in environments where new plugins and apps are disabled by default. In this case, ask the administrator to open the feature.

items.prompt: 2. Am I included in my role?
items.answer: Even if the feature is turned on, it may not be included in your role. If the plugin screen says Disabled by admin, it may be blocked by your workspace settings, role settings, or one of the included apps. In this case, it will ask you to add permissions to your role.

items.prompt: 3. Is the app attached to the plug-in blocked?
items.answer: Even if the plugin is installed, access to the included app may be blocked. This is because installation and app access are evaluated separately. This will ask you to open the role and behavior settings for that app.

items.prompt: 4. Is your connection blocked due to domain restrictions?
items.answer: If your connection to Claude fails during the sign-in step and you are prompted to sign in with your organization's Claude account, verified domain restrictions are the cause. In this case, you will need to connect to your organizational account and not your personal account.

items.prompt: 5. Request to the administrator corresponding to the cause found
items.answer: Once you have found the cause, make a specific request to the person determining the cause. The person who turns it on, the owner who sets the role, and the administrator who sets the organization's policies may be different.

screens.outro: Lastly, let me summarize the main points.

screens.title: Administrator control is divided into functional units
screens.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.

paragraphs: Administrator controls are divided into three units: features, connectors and apps, and shares, and their scope varies by role or organization. The same service is evaluated separately for installation, app access, and permitted actions, so even if one is open, the other may be blocked.

When blocked, I check in order whether the function is turned off, whether it is included in my role, whether the attached app is blocked, or whether there are domain restrictions. Once you find the cause, you can ask the appropriate administrator specifically.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: The fact that the screen varies from person to person is by design. We consider the reasons for the blockage in order from top to bottom.

checks.q: In a ChatGPT managed workspace, a specific plugin is blocked on one employee's screen. What is the first thing to check as the cause?
options: Is access to apps included in the plugin blocked separately?
The employee's laptop operating system version
Is the plugin name translated into Korean?
Number of files in projects created by employees
checks.explain: Even if plug-in installation is allowed, access to the included app may be blocked, so installation, app access, and permission for action are evaluated separately.

wrong.1: Administrator controls are settings that apply to accounts and roles and are not related to the device's operating system.
wrong.2: Display language does not determine access.
wrong.3: The number of project files is independent of plugin permissions.

glossary.def: Control by workspace or organization administrators to turn features and connections on and off.
This is a setting that determines who can use each function.
The scope of apps that your organization allows to connect.
This is a method of tying permissions to roles and assigning roles to each user to determine access.

misconceptions.myth: Once the plugin is installed, you can always use the included apps.
misconceptions.fact: Installation and app access are evaluated separately. Even if the plugin is installed, if you can't access the app that contains the member's role, you won't be able to use features that rely on that app.

misconceptions.myth: The administrator settings for the three products are on the same screen and under the same name.
misconceptions.fact: Location and name vary from product to product. Rather than looking for the name, you need to look for it based on what unit the setting controls.

misconceptions.myth: If you turn off a feature in one service, access to data for that service also disappears.
misconceptions.fact: With Gemini, even if you turn off Gemini from any service, other apps can access that service's data. You need to find out what the range you are turning off is.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Administrator control is divided into features, connectors and apps, and shares.
Coverage varies depending on role and organizational unit.
The same service is evaluated separately for installation, app access, and permitted actions.
We consider the reasons for the blockage in order from top to bottom.
